text: My client was a programmer. He paid me, and handsomely, but toward the end, he started working on the project himself. He didn't pull the repo and ended up sending the wrong request to the server, then didn't pay a large sum of what he owed me because he thought the code was faulty. Plus, he was kind of... emotionally needy; he expected me not to work on any other projects while I was working on his. So here are a few things I've learned from my second project. First, never befriend your client; people who are supposed to pay you make the worst friends. Second, never let your client work on your project. I respect this guy and all, but he was kind of stupid. I told him three times that I had changed the header name in the backend, but he didn't know much about Express, so he thought I was speaking gibberish or something. Sadly, that's why things ended badly between us. Third, never, ever be too available to your client. Set a time, like 7 p.m., and tell them that at exactly that hour you'll be available on Slack, WhatsApp, or whatever to update them on the project. NEVER be at their beck and call 24/7, and don't work on weekends, or they'll get cocky. Fourth, expect a clean, laid-out document detailing what the client wants; don't just ask them. If they decide to change X after you've put a lot of time into it, cite the document. Yeah, cite the fuckers. This dude changed the project over 15 times, and I had to scrap much of my code. In the end, he asked me to rewrite the frontend the way he wanted. I liked his approach, but he didn't pay me for it because he thought it was broken, all because of the header thing I'd told him about three times. Fifth, and this is kind of an extension of the first point: if your client is a programmer, only give him read access to the repo. Sixth, never let your client test the project. Always test it yourself first, and only let your client test it at the end of each cycle, which brings me to my seventh point: set milestones, and always have them pay you at the end of each one. Also, take a retainer, like a quarter of the final fee. I worked with a programmer because I didn't have a published app to my name. I'm going to take a break from working with remote clients, since my professor has found an investor for my chore app, and I'm going to work on it for a month so I have a published app instead of just lines of code. I had two apps when I started working with this guy, but he kind of asserted himself as my ""supervisor"" because he was a programmer himself. Damn, I should never have let that happen. When he worked on the app, he would ruin the repo, and I had to spend two hours every day fixing his mess. He reverted my changes because he believed ""redux-persist is in a loop."" Goddammit, what does that even mean? Okay, I didn't mean to vent, just to relay my experience. If the guy is reading this, please be decent and don't post, because I have proof that you messed up.
